emails.job: Get a cohort-based course operator to create a free Senja account and set up the student testimonial request they have been meaning to send.
emails.single_idea: Asking your students for a testimonial can stop being a message you write, remember and chase: it becomes one form link, with up to three reminders you switch on once, and about half a minute of work on your student's side.
emails.felt_need: People say kind things about the course — in replies, in the group chat, at the end of a module — and none of it is anything I can put on the cohort page. I keep meaning to ask properly and I keep not doing it.
emails.status_quo: Asking by hand, when they happen to remember: a one-off message after a nice comment, and praise otherwise left sitting in threads and replies. Observed in course-creator accounts of collecting student feedback; not established as this reader's workflow, so write it as the familiar habit, not as a fact about them.
emails.why_it_fails: A hand-written ask is one message you have to remember to send, and the follow-up is a second message you have to remember to send — so the ones nobody answers quietly stay unanswered, and the asking only happens when you have spare attention, which during a cohort you don't.
emails.mechanism: The request stops being correspondence and becomes a form. You create the form in a Senja account — sign up with Google or an email address, verify it, give your name, website and plan, and Free is one of the choices — then invite students to it. Turn follow-ups on and Senja sends up to three reminder emails, 1, 3 and 7 days after the original invite, only to the students who haven't responded yet. What lands on the student's side is a personalised page where they write or record their answer; they need no account and no special software, and Senja describes it as taking about 30 seconds. So the thing you set once is the schedule, not the nagging.

alternative_arguments.selection_reason: P2 is the other grounded uncertainty in this audience's research: not only how to ask, but where to collect and display. This bet argues the destination instead of the request — that one student video, once it is in Senja, is hosted and placeable without code or a video host — which gives a cold reader a different reason to act (a home for proof they may already have) rather than a reworded version of the lighter-ask argument. Its evidence, mechanism and payoff are independent of the primary's: nothing here borrows the reminder schedule, the student-side form or the signup facts.
alternative_arguments.argument_issue: The P2 fit is PARTIAL: the product supplies collection, format and display options, but cannot establish which format persuades prospective students, how an embed will look in a specific page template, or what it does to enrolments. The payoff also has a prerequisite — a testimonial has to be in the account first — which belongs in the mechanism, not hidden.

alternative_arguments.felt_need: I've got one or two clips of students saying genuinely useful things, and no idea where they should live. On the cohort page? In the launch emails? Instagram? And I'm not editing video.
alternative_arguments.status_quo: Pasting the quote as plain text or a screenshot onto the cohort page, and putting the occasional video on socials or a third-party host. Common in this category; not established as this reader's current practice, so keep it recognisable rather than asserted.

Once a video testimonial is in the account — collected through a form or imported — it's hosted ad-free inside Senja, and the same testimonial can be added to your website without writing code, used in emails, or remixed into shorter clips for social posts and ads. emails.next_step_value: A free account (Google or an email address, verify it, then your name, website and plan — Free is one of the choices) where they can see the actual request their students would receive: a page where a student writes or records an answer without an account or special software, plus the follow-up setting that sends up to three reminders, 1, 3 and 7 days after the invite, to students who haven't responded.
emails.next_step_limit: Signing up shows them the request and the reminder settings. It does not tell them how many students will reply, whether video or written suits their cohort, or what the result will look like once it's on the page — and it does not lift the Free plan's 15-testimonial limit or unlock the paid-only pieces (welcome videos, branding removal, auto-collect from connected platforms).
emails.subject_strategy: This reader is solution-aware: a subject that argues testimonials matter tells them something they already believe and gets archived. Earn the open on the part they haven't solved — the asking — with one concrete specific rather than a benefit (a link instead of a message, three reminders, half a minute on their side). No invented cohort deadline, no fake urgency, no question that could be answered 'yes, obviously'.

Asking students for testimonials looks like correspondence from the outside: individual messages to write, then a decision about whether to chase the quiet ones. That second part is the one with no obvious end.

It's setup, not correspondence. You write the questions and set each one to writing or video, so the video-or-written question becomes a setting rather than a dilemma. Senja says a simple or multistep collection form takes 60 seconds to create.

Your student gets a personalised page. They write or record their answer there, with no account and no special software — Senja describes that as taking about 30 seconds.
